lines.text: Here's the problem. Our modules are speed-controlled, so they all push about the same.
Equal push means each wheel pushes a quarter of m times a.
A front wheel slips when that's more than mu times its load.
Put in the front load, solve for a, and you get mu g over one plus mu h over x.
With our numbers, that's five point five meters per second squared.
So above five point five, the light front wheels slip, though the whole robot could grip ten.
The heavy back wheels have grip to spare: at ten, two hundred sixty-five newtons each. That takes about one hundred one amps.
When a front wheel slips, the robot falls behind its command, and the back modules push harder, if the current limit lets them.
Sixty amps caps every wheel at one hundred fifty-eight newtons, so the back wheels can't help. That's the twenty twenty-six lesson.
Our code still plans with ten. In our simulator, some wheels slipped, but tag alignment still succeeded ninety-six to ninety-nine percent.
